Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Emeka had been twenty-eight when his convoy halted at the border checkpoint, the dust settling over canvas tents as officials barked orders through cracked megaphones. What remained of that crossing were not long narratives but a series of sharp, frozen frames: a rifle barrel glinting under the midday sun, a stack of stamped passports slipping through a mesh window, his own boots hovering just above cracked earth. He was certain that those moments would never fade, not because they ached in his body, but because they had arrived without warning, demanding immediate attention. Over the following months, he learned to navigate a world that suddenly felt too loud and too demanding. He began to avoid going out when the light was bright, staying inside where the rhythms of his new American home felt steady. He kept his mind occupied at all times, turning over technical manuals on the machinery he would help design, tracing circuits in his head until the silence lost its edge. The patterns of his daily life soon reflected the contours of that early crossing. In his current role as a software engineer, Emeka spent his days surrounded by rows of monitors and the steady hum of server racks, yet the office carried its own quiet authority. The open-plan layout meant that directives traveled quickly, and when a project manager stood at his desk with a tablet, the brief exchange of information often mirrored the swift, unyielding commands of the border officials. He would nod, adjust his glasses, and return to his screen, yet he could feel a familiar beginning to feel detached or unreal, as though the fluorescent lights and the typing colleagues belonged to another room. He avoided other people in the breakroom, preferring to eat alone or step into the stairwell where the concrete walls offered a buffer against sudden conversations. Even now, his apartment reflected that same careful distancing. He kept the curtains drawn during the day, let meals pass without conversation, and filled the quiet hours with word searches and historical documentaries, ensuring that his thoughts never settled long enough to stir. Over the decades, these habits solidified into a steady way of moving through the world. A sudden siren outside could pull his attention sharply upward; a calendar date marked on his wall would make him pause before coffee, as if checking for a ripple in the air. He had come to believe that the past was not somewhere behind him but layered right beside his present. His wife, who had known him since his first decade in the United States, watched him navigate these quiet tides with a familiar patience. She had learned that his stillness was not withdrawal but a practiced rhythm, that his avoidance of social gatherings moved alongside a need to keep the edges of his experience steady. When trauma-related events surfaced—news broadcasts, anniversary weeks, even the particular cadence of a colleague’s voice—Emeka would simply adjust his posture, let the moments pass, and return to his work. Alongside the emotionless recall that accompanied these moments, the visual memories remained crisp. He remembered the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment was a picture in his mind, held in perfect clarity without demanding emotional weight. Now, at seventy-seven, Emeka finds himself standing at a quiet threshold. His colleagues are retiring, his children have moved across the country, and the steady routine of his software engineering career has begun to loosen its grip. His clinical intake placed his symptom burden at a steady forty-four on the screening scale, a score that mapped neatly onto the rhythms he described. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single crisis but a growing awareness that the walls he had built, while protective, had also grown heavy. He hoped, perhaps, to understand why a simple instruction could still make the floor feel slightly unreal beneath his feet, and whether he might allow himself to step outside more often without fear of being pulled back into those old, frozen frames. He does not expect the past to leave him entirely; he only hopes to move through it with the same careful, steady hands that have carried him this far.
